t: Hosea, the only writing prophet from the north
p: Hosea spoke to the northern kingdom, yet his heading names four kings of Judah and only one of Israel.
b: Hosea is the only prophet with a book who came from the northern kingdom, and he speaks to it (Israel, also called Ephraim and Samaria). His name is Hoshea', "he saves", the same word as the name of Israel's last king (2 Kings 17:1) and of Joshua before Moses renamed him (Numbers 13:8). The heading is dated by four kings of Judah, down to Hezekiah, but by only one king of Israel, Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:23-29). Israel had six more kings after him (2 Kings 15:8-17:6). Critics usually say a Judean editor shaped the heading after 722 BC, when the north was gone; others think Hosea simply lived under all five reigns. The oracles themselves point to about 755 to 725 BC.
r: 2 Kings 14:23; 2 Kings 15:8; 2 Kings 17:1; Numbers 13:8; Isaiah 1:1; Micah 1:1

p: The same king of Judah is Azariah in 2 Kings and Uzziah here, in Isaiah, Amos and Chronicles.
b: The Plain English Translation uses "Uzziah" here, as in Isaiah and Amos, because that is the Hebrew name 'Uzziyyah in the heading. The book of Kings calls the same king "Azariah" (2 Kings 15:1), and Chronicles uses both. The two names are close in meaning ("my strength is the LORD" and "the LORD has helped"), and scholars take them as two names for one man. His long reign (about 790 to 740 BC, by the usual dating) overlapped the peace of Jeroboam II.

a: Take a wife of prostitution for yourself
t: Was Hosea's marriage real, a vision, or a story?
p: The Hebrew command is plain; what it meant, and whether it happened, has been argued for two thousand years.
b: A real marriage. Most modern commentators (Wolff, Mays, Andersen and Freedman, Stuart) take it as something Hosea did, though they disagree about the woman: a woman already living by sex, a woman caught up in Baal rites, or an ordinary woman who would later be unfaithful (so that the children are called "of prostitution" in advance). A vision or a parable. Maimonides (Guide 2.46) counts it among prophetic visions, since he held that a prophet's shameful act could not be literal; the Targum, the Aramaic paraphrase, recasts the opening as a command to prophesy to the people. The Talmud takes it as real (Pesachim 87a-b). The medieval commentators Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Kimhi are often reported on this question; this site has not checked them, so none is placed on either side. The Hebrew states it as an act, and the Plain English Translation lets it stand.

p: Hosea's key word zenunim means acts of prostitution; the Plain English Translation keeps that word every time.
b: The Hebrew verb zanah is the ordinary word for a woman who sells sex or has sex outside marriage, and zenunim (1:2; 2:2, 4; 4:12; 5:4) is the plural noun. The Plain English Translation says "prostitution" each time, so the reader sees how often it comes. Adultery is a different word (na'af, 2:2; 3:1; 4:2). Many English versions say "unfaithful" or "adulterous", which are softer and decide what Gomer was. Older books also called her a "sacred" or temple prostitute. That claim now carries little weight: Hebrew has a separate word for shrine women (4:14), and Bird and Budin argue that the evidence for sacred prostitution in ancient Israel and the Near East is weak.
r: Hosea 2:2; Hosea 4:12; Hosea 4:14; Hosea 5:4; Genesis 38:15; Deuteronomy 23:17

p: Only the first child is said to be borne "to him"; the daughter and the second son are not.
b: In the Hebrew, 1:3 says Gomer "bore to him a son". The births in 1:6 and 1:8 say only "a daughter" and "a son", without "to him". Some commentators read this as a hint that the later children were not Hosea's, so that "children of prostitution" in 1:2 would be literal. Others say the phrase may be dropped only for brevity, since 1:6 goes on to say "the LORD said to him". The text does not settle it. The three names, not the fathers, are what the chapter is about.

p: Both names look like ordinary names or word plays; the Talmud plays on them.
b: Gomer comes from a root meaning "to finish" or "to complete"; it is also the name of Japheth's son (Genesis 10:2). Diblaim is a dual form that looks like "two fig cakes" (the word is develah, 1 Samuel 25:18; 30:12). The Talmud (Pesachim 87a-b) plays on both names, and some modern writers hear a sexual pun in them. Others treat them as plain names of a woman from a family or town of that name. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew names and does not read a pun into the translation.

p: The name means "God sows"; it names a valley, a city and a bloody day, and it turns to blessing in 2:22-23.
b: Yizre'el is "God sows" (zara', sow, plus 'el, God). It names a broad valley in the north, a royal city of Israel's kings there (1 Kings 21:1) and, here, the first child. In 1:4 the name carries judgment: sowing as scattering. In 2:22-23 it turns around: "I will sow her for myself in the land." The same name is a threat in the first chapter and a promise in the second, which is why the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew name. In 1:11 "the day of Jezreel" is great.
r: 1 Kings 21:1; 2 Kings 9:30; Hosea 1:5; Hosea 1:11; Hosea 2:22; Hosea 2:23

t: The blood of Jezreel and the house of Jehu
p: Jehu killed Joram, Jezebel and Ahab's family at Jezreel; Hosea says his house will pay.
b: Jehu, anointed by a young prophet whom Elisha sent (2 Kings 9:1-10), killed King Joram and Queen Jezebel and wiped out Ahab's family and followers (2 Kings 9-10). The LORD praised him, promising that his sons would sit on Israel's throne to the fourth generation (2 Kings 10:30). Hosea 1:4 seems to say the opposite. Views: (1) Hosea condemns the massacre itself as excessive; (2) it is not the massacre but the later bloodshed of Jehu's line, which kept Jeroboam's sins (2 Kings 10:31); (3) "Jezreel" stands for royal murder in general, and the coups of 7:3-7 are in view. The dynasty ended when Shallum killed Zechariah son of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 15:10), and the record says: "So came true the word the LORD had spoken to Jehu" (2 Kings 15:12). Swete's Greek has "the house of Judah" where the Hebrew has the house of Jehu; that does not fit the story, and a slip in the Greek text is the likely cause.

t: The bow broken in the Valley of Jezreel
p: The great plain of Jezreel was Israel's battlefield; the text names no battle.
b: The Valley of Jezreel is the wide plain between Galilee and the hills of Samaria, the main road of armies (Judges 6:33; 1 Samuel 29:1). The "bow" stands for Israel's strength in war (compare Hosea 1:7; 2:18). No source names a battle there at the end of the northern kingdom. Some think it points to Tiglath-pileser's conquest of Galilee and the north in 733-732 BC (2 Kings 15:29), others to the general end of the army, and others to a coming reversal of Jehu's coup in the same place. The Plain English Translation does not name a fulfillment.

p: The name means "Not Shown Compassion"; it comes from the word for the womb.
b: Lo-ruhamah is "Not Shown Compassion", or more exactly "Not Shown Compassion" (lo', not, plus the passive of racham, to have compassion). The root is the one behind rachamim, "compassion", and rechem, "womb": the feeling a mother has for the child she bore (1 Kings 3:26). That is why the Plain English Translation says "compassion" and not "mercy". The cancellation is undone in 2:1 ("Ruhamah") and 2:23. The Greek of 2:23 turns it into a word for "loved".

a: save them by the LORD their God
t: How Judah is saved without a bow
p: Judah is promised rescue by the LORD, not by arms; many scholars think this verse was added by a Judean editor.
b: Judah is saved "by the LORD", not by weapons. The usual view of the fulfillment is the rescue of Jerusalem from Sennacherib in 701 BC, when the angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp (2 Kings 19:35), in the days of Hezekiah, who is named in the heading. The Targum reads "by the Word (Memra) of the LORD". Wolff and other critical scholars think 1:7 is a later Judean insertion, because it breaks the pattern of the names; others see it as an original contrast between north and south. The Greek has "sons" where the Hebrew has "house of Judah".

t: "I will not be yours": the reversal of "I Will Be"
p: The Hebrew says "I will not be for you", a reversal of the covenant promise and perhaps of God's name.
b: The Hebrew says ve'anokhi lo' 'ehyeh lakhem, "and I will not be for you", with no "God" in it. Many English versions add "your God". The verb is 'ehyeh, "I will be", the very word of God's name at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14, "I Will Be", with Exodus 3:12). Several scholars hear "I am not 'I Will Be' to you". It is also the covenant formula turned upside down: "I will be your God, and you will be my people" (Leviticus 26:12; compare Exodus 6:7; Jeremiah 7:23). The Plain English Translation leaves the verb alone and does not add "God", so that both the covenant words and the name can be heard. The formula returns in the right order in 2:23.
r: Exodus 3:12; Exodus 3:14; Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 7:23; Hosea 2:23

a: The Israelites will be so many
p: In the Hebrew Bible, 1:10-11 are 2:1-2, and the chapter after that starts two verses later.
b: The English verse numbers used here and in every note follow the KJV. The Hebrew Bible numbers differently at this spot: Hosea 1:10-11 in English is Hosea 2:1-2 in Hebrew, so Hebrew chapter 2 runs from 2:3 to 2:25 and covers English 2:1-23. The promise of Genesis 22:17 and 32:12 (descendants like the sand on the seashore) is turned back on the people who were just named Not My People. The Greek, as printed by Swete, numbers these verses as the English does. The same shift happens again: Hosea 11:12 is Hebrew 12:1, and 13:16 is Hebrew 14:1.

t: Paul reads this verse of the called, Jews and non-Jews
p: In Romans 9:26 Paul quotes this verse after 2:23, and applies both to those God has called.
b: Paul quotes Hosea 2:23 and then 1:10 in Romans 9:25-26, in that order, in a Greek form close to the Septuagint's, with small changes of his own: "there they will be named sons of the living God" (Romans 9:26). He applies them to those God has called "not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles" (compare Romans 9:24). The Hebrew passage is about the northern tribes. Paul, like the Greek, treats "Not My People" as a condition that God can reverse for anyone, which is a reading of the pattern more than of the northern tribes' particular fate. See the "Where Christians differ" card at 2:23.

a: go up out of the land
t: "Go up out of the land": exile, or a rising?
p: Three readings: a return from exile, a new exodus, or a plant rising from the ground.
b: The verb is 'alah, "go up", the word for Israel coming up out of Egypt (2:15) and for going up to Jerusalem. (1) A new exodus or return from exile, led by one head (compare 3:5, "David their king"). (2) A new beginning on the same soil: a plant coming up out of the ground, since the name of the day is Jezreel, "God sows" (a reading that fits the name; no commentator is cited for it here). (3) Going up to battle, which fits no other verse in the chapter. The "one head" is not named. Many scholars think 1:10-2:1 is a later hope added after the fall of Samaria; others see it as Hosea's own answer to his judgments. The Targum speaks of the exiles being gathered.

p: These are the names Lo-ammi and Lo-ruhamah with the "Not" taken away.
b: 'Ammi is "my people" and Ruhamah is "Shown Compassion", the two names of 1:6 and 1:9 with lo', "not", removed. The Plain English Translation keeps them as names so that the reader sees the cancellation. The plural "brothers" and "sisters" are the children of the mother of 2:2, the people of Israel, and they are told to speak to each other by the new names before they take their mother to court. The Greek turns the names into common words: "my people" and "she who is shown mercy".

a: Bring a case against your mother
p: The verb riv means to bring a legal case; the mother is the nation and the children are its people.
b: Riv is the legal word for bringing a charge, and rib is a lawsuit. The prophets often make God the plaintiff in a case against his people, with heaven and earth as witnesses (Isaiah 1:2; Micah 6:1-2; Jeremiah 2:9); the pattern is called the "covenant lawsuit" (Huffmon). Here the children are told to accuse the mother, and the "mother" is Israel as a whole. The words "she is not my wife, and I am not her husband" sound like the formula for ending a marriage, which has matching words in Aramaic marriage contracts from Elephantine in Egypt (fifth century BC). They may be a formal divorce, or a warning before one, since the next lines offer a way back ("Let her take her prostitution away").

t: The woman in the lawsuit: metaphor and critique
p: Hosea 2 pictures Israel as an unfaithful wife; feminist scholars ask what that picture does to women.
b: The mother is Israel, and her "lovers" are the gods and nations she follows. Since the 1980s many scholars (Setel, Weems, Yee) have argued that the picture presents a violent husband as God and a naked, shamed woman as the sinner, and gives her no voice; the language of 2:3, 2:10 and 2:12 is read as abuse, and as a pattern that has been used to excuse abuse. Others (Ortlund, Keefe, Kelle, Moughtin-Mumby) answer that it is a metaphor aimed at Israel's men and leaders, that the shaming is a threat and not a command, and that the chapter ends in her restoration (2:14-23). The critics reply that the restoration is still on the husband's terms. The Plain English Translation does not soften the text.

t: Stripping, exposure and the husband's duties
p: Stripping was a public shaming of a woman; here it is also a husband withdrawing food and clothes.
b: Stripping an unfaithful woman is a threat in other prophets too (Ezekiel 16:37-39; Jeremiah 13:22, 26). Here it joins a second idea: a husband owed his wife food, clothing and her rights as a wife (Exodus 21:10). The threat is to withdraw them, the grain, wool and flax of 2:5 and 2:9, and to return her to the state of the day she was born. The dry wilderness in the second half of the verse is where she began (2:14-15). Whether this is law, metaphor or a poet's anger is argued; it is shocking in every reading.

p: The lovers are the Baals who were thought to give grain, wine and wool, and also the nations Israel sought as allies.
b: In Canaanite belief Baal was the storm god who gave rain, grain, wine and oil, which is why the woman says her lovers give her food, water, wool, flax, oil and drink (compare 2:8, 2:12). The same word, "lovers", is used of the nations Israel sent for in 8:9 ("Ephraim has hired lovers") and of the allies in Jeremiah 22:20 and Ezekiel 16:33-37. Many scholars hold that Hosea means both at once, since to him the worship of Baal and the courting of Assyria and Egypt were one fault: trust in someone other than the LORD. The Plain English Translation keeps the single word.

a: fence your road in with thorns
p: A road hedged with thorns and a wall keeps a person from the way she wants to take.
b: Hedging a road is a picture of blocking someone's way. Job complains that God has hedged him in (Job 3:23), and the poet of Lamentations says God walled him in and made his path crooked (Lamentations 3:7, 9). Here the woman follows her lovers and finds she cannot get to them (2:7). The grammar shifts from "your road" to "her wall"; the Greek makes all of it third person, but the shift is common in prophetic poetry and the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. The picture reads either as punishment or, in the next verse, as a mercy that makes her turn around.

a: Let me go back to my first husband
t: Her return is for what she can get (Claude's theory)
p: Her plan to return is made out of need; God's answer in 2:14 does not wait for a better motive.
b: Claude's theory. Notice the reason she gives: "it went well for me then, better than now." She does not say she was wrong. She says she was better fed. The same shape comes back in 6:1-3, where the people return because the LORD will heal and send rain, and in 7:14, where they cry out over grain and new wine. In each case the return follows need, and each time the LORD answers differently: here by leading her out to the wilderness (2:14), in 6:4 with "What can I do with you?" The book may be showing that the LORD's first move comes before a good motive does. This overlaps with the many commentators who read 6:1-3 as a shallow return. It rests on 2:7, 6:1-3 and 7:14 and cannot be proved.

p: The Hebrew says the silver and gold were made "for the Baal" or into an image of him.
b: The Hebrew is 'asu laba'al, "they made [it] for/into the Baal". With the Plain English Translation's "into Baal" the gold and silver become the god, an image such as the golden calves of Bethel (1 Kings 12:28-30) or the image of Judges 17:3-4. Other versions say "used for Baal", meaning offerings or temple furnishings. The point is clear either way: the LORD gave the grain, the new wine and the oil (the standard list of the land's produce, Deuteronomy 7:13), and the woman sent the gift on to someone else. In 2:13 and 2:17 the Hebrew has "the Baals", plural.

p: The Hebrew nablut appears only here; it is related to words for foolish and shameful acts.
b: Nablut is found nowhere else in the Bible. It comes from the root of nabal, "fool", and nevalah, a shameful, senseless act, the word used of the rape at Gibeah (Judges 19:23) and of Shechem's crime against Dinah (Genesis 34:7). Translators have chosen "lewdness", "genitals", "shame" and "folly". The Greek has "uncleanness". The Plain English Translation says "naked folly" to keep both the "fool" root and the uncovering, and so that the reader can tell this word from the ordinary words for "shame" (4:7, 4:18), which are different Hebrew words. Whatever the exact word, the threat is exposure in front of the lovers who will not help her, and the picture is shocking by design.

p: The LORD's own feasts end, because they have been mixed with the days of the Baals.
b: The list of festival, new moon, sabbath and appointed feast covers Israel's whole calendar of joy. The same list appears in Isaiah's complaint that the LORD cannot stand them together with wrongdoing (Isaiah 1:13). Here the feasts stop, and in 2:13 they are called "the days of the Baals". Whether Israel kept the LORD's feasts while giving Baal the credit for the harvest, or kept Baal's feasts under the LORD's calendar, the text does not say. Hosea 9:5 asks what the people will do on the day of the festival.

t: "My pay": the price of a prostitute
p: The Hebrew 'etnah means a payment for sex; she calls the harvest her fee from the lovers.
b: 'Etnah is a form of 'etnan, the "fee" of a prostitute that may not be brought into the LORD's house (Deuteronomy 23:18), and a related word is used in 9:1. She believes her vines and fig trees, the signs of peace and plenty (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4), were pay from her lovers. The LORD's answer is to make them a thicket (the vineyard of Isaiah 5:5-6 faces the same threat) for wild animals to eat. The Greek reads "my payments" in the same sense.

p: Baal had many local forms; the Plain English Translation says "the Baals" when the Hebrew is plural.
b: Ba'al means "lord" or "owner", and the storm and fertility god of Canaan was worshiped in many places, each with its own Baal (the Baal of Peor, Numbers 25:3; the Baal of Berith, Judges 8:33). So the Hebrew has "the Baals" here and in 2:17, and the Plain English Translation follows it. The same plural is in Judges 2:11 and 1 Samuel 7:4. The "ring" (nezem) is a nose ring or an earring (Genesis 24:47 and 35:4); the woman dresses up for the festivals. The phrase "the days of the Baals" ties this verse to 2:11.

p: The Hebrew verb can mean to persuade, to seduce or to trick; each is used for this verse.
b: Pittah is the verb of persuading, with a shade of weakness or foolishness in it. It is used of a man who lures a young woman into sex (Exodus 22:16), of Delilah's enticing of Samson (Judges 16:5) and of the LORD enticing Jeremiah (Jeremiah 20:7, "You enticed me, LORD, and I was enticed"). In Hosea it is a courtship: the LORD leads her out to the wilderness and "speaks to her heart", as a man speaks to win a woman (Genesis 34:3; Ruth 2:13). The English word "coax" keeps the gentleness and the hint of pressure. Readers have taken it as tender love, as a husband's manipulation, or as both, since it comes right after the threats of 2:3-13.

a: the Valley of Achor as a door of hope
p: Achor, "trouble", is where Achan was stoned; Hosea makes it the doorway into the land.
b: After Jericho, Achan took things set apart for the LORD, and Israel lost the battle at Ai. Joshua brought Achan up to the valley and said, "Why have you brought trouble on us?" and Israel stoned him (Joshua 7:25). "That is why the name of that place is the Valley of Achor to this day" (Joshua 7:26). Achor means "trouble". The valley lies on the northern border of Judah near Jericho (Joshua 15:7), at the entrance to the land from the wilderness. Hosea turns the place of the first trouble in the land into a door of hope, and Isaiah later does the same (Isaiah 65:10). The wilderness road of 2:14 ends there. Swete's Greek has the valley "to open her understanding" (dianoixai synesin autēs) where the Hebrew has "a door of hope".
orig: עֵמֶק עָכוֹר לְפֶתַח תִּקְוָה ('emeq 'akhor lefetach tiqvah)

t: "She will answer": the Hebrew verb has several meanings
p: 'Anah can mean answer, respond, sing, or be humbled; the Greek chose "be humbled".
b: 'Anah first means "answer", and the Plain English Translation keeps that, because the same verb opens the chain of answering in 2:21-22. It can also mean to sing in turn, as Miriam did (Exodus 15:21), or to testify. A second verb with the same letters means to be bowed down or humbled, and the Greek has "she will be humbled" (Swete's text). In every reading the day of the exodus is the model: she met the LORD in the wilderness, and Israel sang (Exodus 15).

a: came up from the land of Egypt
p: Hosea and Jeremiah both remember the first days after the exodus as Israel's youth and engagement.
b: Here the exodus is the day Israel was young, and the wilderness is the time of the first love. Jeremiah says the same: "the loyal love of your youth" (Jeremiah 2:2). Other prophets remember the wilderness more harshly (Ezekiel 20:10-21; Amos 5:25), and so does the book of Numbers. So the earlier days are a pattern the LORD can renew, not a golden age to be copied. Hosea speaks of a second wilderness and a second exodus (compare 11:1, 11).

t: "My husband" and "My Baal": a play on words
p: Both words mean "my husband"; the second is the name of the god.
b: 'Ishi is "my man, my husband", and ba'li is "my owner, my husband". Both are used for a husband in Hebrew law and story (Exodus 21:3, 22; Deuteronomy 24:4), and Jeremiah has the LORD say "I am your husband" with the verb from the same root (Jeremiah 3:14). So the problem is not the meaning of "Baal" as "husband" but the name, which belongs to a god. The LORD asks to be called by the word that carries love and not rule. In the next verse the names of the Baals are removed from her mouth.

t: A covenant with the animals, and no war
p: Peace with the wild animals and the end of war are the signs of a restored creation.
b: In the flood story God made a covenant with every living creature (Genesis 9:9-10), and the prophets picture the end of violence between humans and animals and between nations (Isaiah 11:6-9; Isaiah 2:4; Ezekiel 34:25; Zechariah 9:10). The beasts that were to eat her vines (2:12) now keep the peace. The list of wild animals, birds and creeping things matches Genesis 1:24 and 9:2; the breaking of bow, sword and war is a promise like Psalm 46:9. Safety is the old covenant blessing of Leviticus 26:5-6.

p: A betrothal was a legal promise with a price; the LORD names the gifts in the next words.
b: 'Eras is "to betroth", the legal promise to marry that came before the wedding and bound the couple (Deuteronomy 20:7; 22:23-24). It was sealed with the bride-price (mohar, Exodus 22:16). The verb comes three times in 2:19-20, with "forever" the first time. Many scholars hear the gifts that follow as the price: righteousness, justice, loyal love, compassion, faithfulness. Jewish practice has men say these lines (Hosea 2:21-22 in the Hebrew numbering) while winding the strap of the arm tefillin around the finger, as the prayer book sets out.

t: Whose gifts are righteousness, justice, loyal love and compassion?
p: The gifts may come from the LORD to the people, or be the qualities he asks of them.
b: Two readings. (1) God's gifts: the LORD pays the bride-price, giving what the marriage needs, his own righteousness, justice, loyal love and compassion. (2) The qualities of the new marriage: the couple will be bound in these ways, and the people will practice them (compare 12:6). The Plain English Translation's "righteousness and justice" matches the pair in Isaiah and Amos (Isaiah 5:7; Amos 5:24); "loyal love" (hesed) and "compassion" (rachamim) are the marks of the LORD in Exodus 34:6 and the root of the name in 1:6. The answer "both" is common: what he gives he asks back.

p: To know the LORD is the book's central hope; "know" in Hebrew means to be close and faithful, not only to be told facts.
b: Yada', "to know", is also the word used for sexual intimacy, and in Hosea it names the relationship the whole book is about. Israel has "no knowledge of God" (4:1), a spirit of prostitution keeps them from knowing the LORD (5:4), and the LORD wants knowledge of God more than burnt offerings (6:6). Jeremiah sets the meaning beside justice: "He took up the case of the poor and the needy; then all was well. Is this not knowing me?" (Jeremiah 22:16). The Plain English Translation uses "knowledge of God" for da'at 'elohim every time.
r: Hosea 4:1; Hosea 4:6; Hosea 5:4; Hosea 6:3; Hosea 6:6; Jeremiah 22:16

p: Heaven answers earth, earth answers the crops and the crops answer Jezreel: a rain and harvest chain.
b: The answers run from the sky down: the LORD answers the heavens (they ask for rain), the heavens answer the earth, the earth answers the grain, the new wine and the oil, and these answer "Jezreel", the people now sown ("God sows"). It reverses the loss in 2:8-12, where the LORD took back the grain and the wine. The rain, in Canaanite belief the gift of Baal, is here the LORD's answer. Jezreel, once the name of a curse, now receives the harvest.

t: "Sow": planting the people in the land
p: To sow is the picture of resettling: the people are seed, and the name Jezreel means "God sows".
b: Zara', "sow", is the root of the name Jezreel, and the LORD now sows the woman in the land for himself. Other prophets use the same picture of replanting: "I will sow seed in the house of Israel and the house of Judah" (Jeremiah 31:27); Amos 9:15 says they will not be pulled up again. "For myself" (li) is the same word that closes each of the betrothal lines in 2:19-20. The Greek has "I will sow her for myself on the earth", a small difference with the same sense.

p: Romans 9:25 and 1 Peter 2:10 take this verse to be about people who were not God's people and now are.
b: Paul quotes the verse in Romans: "I will call 'my people' those who are not my people, and 'loved' her who was not loved" (Romans 9:25). He adapts the Greek. Swete's text has "I will love Not Loved, and I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'", and Paul writes "I will call" (kalesō) in place of "I will say" and keeps the Greek "loved" for Ruhamah, so "compassion" becomes "love" without changing the line's force. First Peter 2:10 echoes the same two names for its readers, who were once "not a people". For Paul and Peter the pattern of Hosea (the nation rejected and called back) now shapes how God treats those outside Israel. Whether the church replaces, includes or joins Israel in this reading is one of the great divides; see the card below and the topic on the church and Israel.

a: a woman who is loved by a companion
t: Is the woman of chapter 3 Gomer?
p: The Hebrew says only "a woman"; whether she is the wife of chapter 1 is argued.
b: The same woman. "Again" in the first line, and the sequence of chapters 1 to 3, suggest Gomer, now living with another man, bought back by her husband; this has been the common view in older and recent commentaries. A second woman. The text says "a woman", not "your wife", and chapter 3 tells in the first person what chapter 1 told in the third; some think two separate acts (or one act told twice). One event told twice. A few scholars read chapters 1 and 3 as two accounts of one marriage. The Hebrew phrase "loved by a companion" can also be read "loving evil" (as in the Greek), so the Plain English Translation's choice is itself uncertain; see the variant. The commentaries in the source list lay out all three.

p: Pressed raisin cakes were food at feasts, and they were used in worship of other gods.
b: 'Ashishe 'anavim, "cakes of grapes", are pressed raisin cakes, a festive food (2 Samuel 6:19; Song of Songs 2:5). Jeremiah 7:18 describes women kneading dough for cakes for the Queen of Heaven. So the phrase "love raisin cakes" may point to feasts of other gods, or simply to love of the good things the harvest festivals brought. The Greek translates "cakes with raisins". The line makes the point that Israel loves the gifts more than the Giver, as the woman in 2:5 loved her lovers for the food.
r: 2 Samuel 6:19; Song of Songs 2:5; Jeremiah 7:18; Hosea 2:5

t: The price: a slave's price, a bride-price, or a ransom?
p: Fifteen shekels of silver plus about a homer and a half of barley may add up to thirty shekels, the price of a slave.
b: The text says "fifteen of silver" and the word "shekels" is supplied. A homer of barley was about a donkey's load, and the lethech (only here in the Bible) is usually taken as half a homer. Some commentators add the barley's value to the silver to reach thirty shekels, the compensation for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), though the text does not do the sum. Others call the payment a bride-price (mohar) or the price of freeing her from a debt or from a man who held her. The verb karah means to acquire or buy. The Greek has "hired" and "a nebel of wine" instead of the second barley measure.

t: "And also I to you": a short, unclear line
p: The Hebrew has no verb: "and also I [am] to you". It may mean he will wait for her as she waits for him.
b: The line is vegam 'ani 'elayikh, "and also I to you", with the verb left out. (1) Mutual faithfulness: as she must not belong to another man, so he will not belong to another woman, nor to her. (2) Mutual waiting: he will abstain from her also, for the days of her probation. (3) Promise: I will be toward you as I will be (compare 1:9, "I will not be yours", now turned). The Plain English Translation leaves the verb out, as the Hebrew does, and so does not choose among these. The "many days" and the verb "stay" are taken up for Israel in the next verse.

t: What the list takes away, the legitimate and the forbidden
p: The loss of king, prince, sacrifice, pillar, ephod and teraphim covers both permitted and forbidden things.
b: The six things lost make three pairs: king and prince (the state), sacrifice and pillar (the shrine), ephod and teraphim (ways of getting an answer from God or the gods). Some of these the law approved (kings, sacrifice, the priest's ephod, Exodus 28), and some it forbade (the standing stone, Deuteronomy 16:22; the teraphim, 1 Samuel 15:23; 2 Kings 23:24). So the list does not blame; it describes exile, a time with no kings, no worship and no divination of any kind. An ephod is a priestly garment or an image (Judges 8:27; 17:5), and teraphim are household gods or oracle images (Genesis 31:19). The exile of the north after 722 BC is the usual setting. The Greek (Swete) has a different list after "sacrifice": "altar" (thysiastērion), "priesthood" (hierateia) and "revealing things" (dēloi), in the places of the pillar, the ephod and the teraphim.

t: "David their king": a Judean addition, or the Messiah?
p: Many critics think 3:5 was added by a Judean editor; Jews and Christians have read "David" as the Messiah.
b: The northern prophet speaks of David, king of Judah, and of the Davidic line: for the north, that is a return to the house they left in 1 Kings 12. Many critical scholars (Wolff among them) therefore see "and David their king", or all of 3:5, as a later Judean addition; others hold that Hosea himself looked for the reunion of the tribes (1:11). Jewish readers took it as the Messiah: the Targum reads "they will obey Messiah the son of David, their king". Christian readers have taken it as Christ (Jerome; Cyril of Alexandria), and some dispensationalist readers connect it to the future restoration of Israel. The Plain English Translation says "David their king", as the Hebrew does.

p: The phrase means "in the afterward of the days"; it can mean a later time or the end.
b: Be'acharit hayyamim is, literally, "in the after-part of the days". It means the future that follows the days being described, whether near or far. Jacob uses it in Genesis 49:1 for what will happen to his sons' tribes, and Isaiah for the nations coming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2, "In the days to come"). Christian readers often make it "the last days" in the sense of the end of time or of the age begun by Christ. In Hosea it follows the exile and the return (3:5a), so the time is not named more closely.

t: The LORD's lawsuit against the land
p: Chapter 4 opens like a court summons; the charge is the lack of three things, listed in the next lines.
b: The words "hear the word of the LORD" and "a case" (riv) mark a covenant lawsuit, as in 2:2 and 12:2; Micah 6:1-2 and Isaiah 1:2-3 open the same way (Huffmon). The accused are "those who live in the land", all the people, and the charge is that three covenant qualities are missing. The speaker is the LORD, who is both prosecutor and judge. The next verses list crimes that break the Ten Commandments (4:2), then turn on the priests (4:4-10). From here to chapter 14 the oracles are not arranged by date, and many are short and hard to place.

a: faithfulness or loyal love or knowledge of God
t: Faithfulness, loyal love, knowledge of God
p: Three covenant qualities the book keeps returning to; all three are missing.
b: 'Emet ("faithfulness", also "truth"), hesed ("loyal love") and da'at 'elohim ("knowledge of God") sum up what the LORD wanted from Israel. The first two are the pair that describe the LORD himself: "great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). The third, "knowledge of God", is not information. Jeremiah 22:16 ties it to defending the poor, and Hosea 6:6 sets it beside loyal love. A people that lacks these things has lost the relationship, not only the facts. The Plain English Translation uses "loyal love" for human hesed in 4:1 and 6:4, 6 as well as for the LORD's, so the reader can see the match.
orig: אֱמֶת חֶסֶד דַּעַת אֱלֹהִים ('emet chesed da'at 'elohim)

t: The Ten Commandments in a list
p: Cursing, lying, murder, stealing and adultery echo the commandments, in a different order.
b: The five words echo the commandments against false oaths (Exodus 20:7), lying witness, murder, stealing and adultery (Exodus 20:13-16). The Hebrew 'alah means swearing, often a false or cursing oath. Jeremiah 7:9 uses a similar list: stealing, murder, adultery, swearing falsely. Here the order is different from the commandments, and the point is that the whole list "breaks out" (paratsu) like water through a wall, until blood touches blood. The sins are those of the whole land, not only of the king.

p: The Hebrew verb can come from "mourn" or "dry up"; the Plain English Translation follows Jeremiah 12:4 and the Greek.
b: The verb te'evel comes either from 'avel, "mourn", or from a second verb "dry up", "wither". The Greek has "the land will mourn", and Jeremiah 12:4 asks, "How long must the land mourn?". The next word, "withers", suits dryness as well. Human sin is shown to spoil the land, the animals and even the fish, a link of crime and creation heard in Jeremiah 4:23-28 and Isaiah 24:4-6. The mention of the fish of the sea is rare: few passages widen the judgment as far (Zephaniah 1:3; compare Ezekiel 38:20 and, for the fear that falls on the animals, Genesis 9:2).
r: Jeremiah 12:4; Jeremiah 4:23; Isaiah 24:4; Zephaniah 1:3; Ezekiel 38:20; Genesis 9:2

t: Who is accused in 4:4? The text is uncertain
p: The Hebrew reads "your people are like those who bring a case against a priest"; the sense is uncertain.
b: The Hebrew is hard. (1) As written: the priest is the one accused, and the people are so bad that they are "like those who bring a case against a priest", a crime in Deuteronomy 17:12. (2) Changing one word: "for my case is with you, priest" (immekha rivi), which many scholars prefer because the speech turns to the priest in 4:5. (3) The Greek reads "my people are like a priest who is spoken against". The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic Text as it stands and gives the Greek and the emended text in the variant. From 4:4 to 4:10 the target is the priesthood.

p: The mother is the nation or the priesthood's line; the Greek has a different verb.
b: "Mother" is the word of 2:2 for the nation, seen as the parent of its people. The verb damiti is "I will destroy" or "I will silence" (the root damah II). The Greek reads the verb as "liken": "I have compared your mother to the night". In either case the priest is told that his class and his people will go down with him; "day" and "night" mean always. This is the first verse in which the prophets themselves are blamed, a charge that returns in 9:7-8 and 12:10.

a: My people are destroyed because they have no knowledge
p: A famous line; the accusation is aimed first at the priests, whose job was to teach.
b: In the Hebrew nidmu can mean "destroyed" or "silenced" (the Greek has "made like", reading a different sense of the root). The knowledge in question is hada'at, "the knowledge", the knowledge of God and the teaching of the law that the priests were to give (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10; Malachi 2:7). The people are destroyed because the priests did not teach them, and the LORD answers by removing the priests. Applied to the church, the line has been used to argue for learning and for preaching; its first target is the priestly class of Bethel and the north.
orig: נִדְמוּ עַמִּי מִבְּלִי הַדָּעַת (nidmu 'ammi mibbeli hadda'at)

p: Torah here is the priests' spoken instruction, the teaching they were to give the people.
b: Torah means "instruction" and, from there, "law". Where it refers to a priest's or prophet's oral teaching, the Plain English Translation says "teaching" (as in Isaiah 1:10; 2:3; 8:16). Here the priests are told that they "forgot the teaching of your God", the very thing they were supposed to give: they were to teach the people the LORD's decisions (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10). The punishment fits the crime: you forgot, so I will forget. The phrase "forget your children" shows how far a priest's failure reaches.

a: I will trade their glory for shame
p: Psalm 106:20 and Jeremiah 2:11 say the people traded their glory; Hosea says the LORD will trade it back.
b: Psalm 106:20 says Israel "traded their glory for the shape of an ox that feeds on grass", and Jeremiah 2:11 says "my people have traded their Glory for something that cannot help." Hosea 4:7 uses the same verb and the same word for glory, but now God is the one who makes the exchange, and it goes the other way, from glory to shame. The Masoretic Text and the Dead Sea scroll 4Q78 (4QXIIc) read "I will exchange" ('amir). The Greek has "I will set their glory to dishonor" (thēsomai, "I will set"), not "exchange". A guess sometimes made is that the original was "they exchanged their glory", as in the psalm and Jeremiah, and that it was changed so that the verse would not say that the people had changed God's glory; no manuscript has that reading. This site has not checked whether a rabbinic list of scribal corrections includes this verse, so none is cited.

a: They feed on the sin of my people
p: The same Hebrew word means "sin" and "sin offering", and the priests ate the sin offerings.
b: Chatta't means both "sin" and "sin offering". Priests ate part of the meat of the sin offerings people brought (Leviticus 6:26; 10:17). Hosea's line, "they eat the sin of my people", is a bitter pun on this custom: the more sin there was, the more they had to eat, so they "hunger for their guilt" ('avon). Many commentators take this as a charge that the priests wanted the people to go on sinning. The idea fits the accusation of 4:7, "as they grew in number, so they sinned".

t: A sentence that crosses the verse break
p: The Hebrew sentence ends in the next verse, so the English verse ends on a dangling "to keep up".
b: The Masoretic verse division ends 4:10 on the word "to keep" (lishmor), and 4:11 begins with "prostitution". Read together they say the people left the LORD to keep up prostitution. The Greek takes the same words differently: "they left off keeping the LORD" and joins "prostitution" to 4:11 as a noun beginning a new list. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew verse numbers and lets the sentence run across them. The alternative is to put "prostitution" at the end of 4:10; nothing else in the Hebrew changes.

t: Asking wood and sticks for answers
p: The people ask a wooden thing for advice; the practice is a kind of divination.
b: The "wood" may be a sacred tree or pole (an Asherah), an idol carved of wood (Jeremiah 2:27; Habakkuk 2:19), or a divination stick. The "stick" (maqqel) is a walking staff, thrown or watched for signs (a practice called rhabdomancy); Ezekiel 21:21 describes the king of Babylon shaking arrows and reading the liver. The Greek speaks of "signs" and "rods". The charge is that Israel asks things for guidance when it should ask the LORD, who has prophets (compare 12:10). The same verse blames a "spirit of prostitution", an impulse that leads people away.

t: Shrines on the hills under the trees
p: The high places were hilltop shrines with trees and standing stones; the shade was part of the worship.
b: Canaanite and Israelite open-air shrines stood on hilltops, often with a tree, a standing stone and an Asherah pole (1 Kings 14:23, "on every high hill and under every leafy tree"). Kings and priests were told to destroy them (Deuteronomy 12:2-3; 2 Kings 18:4). The three trees are the oak, the poplar (Genesis 30:37) and the terebinth. "Good" shade also suggests the comfort of the festival. The sexual language that follows (daughters and brides) is bitter: the women do what the men do at the same shrines (4:14). See the topics on high places and standing stones.

p: Qedeshot means "holy" or "set-apart" women; whether they were prostitutes is disputed.
b: Qedeshah means "a holy woman", a woman attached to a shrine. Genesis 38:21 uses it for the woman Tamar poses as, and Deuteronomy 23:17 bans a "shrine woman" and a "shrine man" from Israel. Hosea sets it beside "prostitutes" (zonot). Older books called them "sacred prostitutes" in Baal's fertility rites; today Bird and Budin doubt that such a class existed and think the word describes women doing some other service at shrines, or that Hosea uses it as an insult. The Plain English Translation says "shrine women", as in Deuteronomy, and leaves the question open.

a: I will not hold your daughters to account
t: Why the women are not punished
p: God says he will not punish the daughters, because the men are the worse offenders.
b: Three readings. (1) The men are worse: the women are not held to account because the fathers and husbands go to the same shrines; the line shifts blame to men, which some feminist readers welcome. (2) A hard saying: God leaves them to their own sin, which is itself the punishment (compare 4:17). (3) A question: "Shall I not hold them to account?" A few commentators read it this way, but the Hebrew has no question mark. The following words ("for the men themselves go off with prostitutes") fit the first reading best. The line is also a warning that women's actions are being reported to shame the men.

t: Gilgal and Beth-aven: shrines of the north
p: Beth-aven means "house of wickedness"; it is Bethel by a pun.
b: Beth-aven is "house of wickedness" or "house of nothing". It is a play on Bethel, "house of God", where Jeroboam I set up one of two golden calves (1 Kings 12:28-30). A town named Beth-aven also stood near Bethel (Joshua 7:2; 18:12), but Hosea uses the name for the shrine itself (5:8; 10:5, 8). Gilgal was Israel's first camp in the land and a northern shrine (Joshua 4; 1 Samuel 11:14-15), which Amos names along with Bethel (Amos 4:4; 5:5). Hosea tells Judah to keep away from both and to avoid the oath "As the LORD lives" sworn at such places (compare Amos 8:14).
r: Joshua 7:2; Joshua 18:12; 1 Kings 12:28; Amos 4:4; Amos 5:5; Hosea 9:15; Hosea 10:5; Hosea 12:11

a: Can the LORD now pasture them
t: A question, a statement or a threat?
p: The line can be a question ("can the LORD pasture them like a lamb?"), a threat, or a grim promise.
b: The Hebrew has no question mark. (1) A question whose answer is no: a stubborn heifer cannot be grazed like a lamb in a quiet meadow (the Plain English Translation's reading). (2) A threat: the LORD will let them out into the open, scattered like sheep without a shepherd, so that exile is the "broad pasture". (3) A promise: in the Greek the sentence is a statement, "now the LORD will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place". The heifer image returns in 10:11, where Ephraim is a trained heifer who liked to thresh.

t: Ephraim, Israel, Jacob, Samaria: the names of the north
p: Ephraim, the biggest northern tribe, stands for the whole northern kingdom.
b: Hosea uses "Ephraim" more than thirty times for the northern kingdom, and he mixes it with "Israel", "Jacob" and "Samaria" (the capital). Ephraim was the leading tribe of the north, from Joseph's younger son blessed over Manasseh (Genesis 48:19-20), and Jeroboam I came from it. So "Ephraim" is the nation's usual name in Isaiah 7:2, 5, 8, 9 as well. The Plain English Translation keeps "Ephraim" and "Israel" as the Hebrew has them and does not turn one into the other. "Israel" without help can also mean the whole people, north and south; Hosea uses it both ways.

p: The imperative may be God speaking to the prophet, or the prophet to Judah, and it means abandonment.
b: The Hebrew is hanach lo, "leave him" or "let him rest". Who is addressed? The prophet, told to stop pleading (compare Jeremiah 7:16); Judah, told to keep away; or the LORD telling himself. Whatever the speaker, the effect is abandonment as judgment: the idol-lover is given what he wants. Paul later says the same of Gentiles, whom God "handed over" to what their hearts desired (Romans 1:24). The idols ('atsabbim) are literally "hurtful things", from a root for pain.

a: Her shields love shame, yes, love it
t: Hosea 4:18: one of the hardest verses
p: The Hebrew words are unclear; the Greek and the English versions all differ.
b: The Hebrew reads, roughly, sar sov'am hazneh hiznu 'ahavu hav qalon maginneha. "Their drink" (sov'am) may be a different word altogether; "has run out" or "has turned sour" (sar) is a guess; "love" and "give" ('ahavu havu) may be one repeated word; "her shields" are rulers (Psalm 47:9, "the shields of the earth"), and "shame" may be "shame" or the Greek's "dishonor". The Greek reads, "he chose Canaanites; they went on prostituting themselves". The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic consonants and picks the most likely sense, and says plainly that the verse is uncertain.
orig: סָר סָבְאָם הַזְנֵה הִזְנוּ אָהֲבוּ הֵבוּ קָלוֹן מָגִנֶּיהָ

a: A wind has bound her up in its wings
p: The wind carries the nation off and leaves its altars to shame it.
b: "Wind" (ruach) also means "spirit", and the same word was just used for the "spirit of prostitution" (4:12). The picture is of a storm that wraps a person up and carries her away, as the Assyrian army or exile will do. It prepares the sentence in 8:7, "they sow the wind". The final "sacrifices" in the Masoretic vowels are "altars" in the Greek; the consonants are the same. Whether the altars bring shame or the sacrifices do, the shrines Israel trusted fail it.

t: Mizpah and Tabor: traps for the people
p: Mizpah and Tabor were places of ambush and perhaps of shrines; the three audiences are priests, people and royal house.
b: The call goes to three groups: the priests, the house of Israel (the people) and the house of the king. Two high places are named. Mizpah ("lookout") is a common place name, in Benjamin (Judges 20:1) and in Gilead (Judges 11:29); Tabor is the round mountain at the edge of the Jezreel plain (Judges 4:6). A "trap" and a "net" are hunters' tools. Either the leaders waylaid pilgrims at these sites, or they lured the people into worship there. The Greek translates Mizpah as "the lookout" and Tabor as "Itabyrion" and does not decide.

p: God knows Ephraim fully (5:3); Ephraim does not know the LORD (5:4).
b: The verb yada' that means "know" in 2:20, 4:1 and 5:4 is here God's knowledge of his people. Nothing is hidden from him, in the sense of Psalm 139 and Amos 3:2, where Israel alone is "known" among the families of the earth. The two knowings are meant to be joined, but only one side keeps its part. The line "Israel is not hidden from me" may be a comfort or a threat, depending on whether the listener is hiding.

a: A spirit of prostitution lives inside them
p: The "spirit" is an inner drive, not a demon; the same phrase is in 4:12.
b: Ruach zenunim, "a spirit of prostitution", is an impulse or disposition that grips a person from inside and "leads astray" (4:12). Other writers speak of a "spirit of confusion" (Isaiah 19:14), a "spirit of deep sleep" (Isaiah 29:10) and a lying spirit (1 Kings 22:22). The English "spirit" does not decide whether the writer thinks of a being or of a mood. The result is that deeds, not knowledge or intention only, "do not let them turn back": habit has become a chain.

t: "Israel's pride": the nation's arrogance, or a title of God?
p: The Hebrew ge'on Yisra'el is usually Israel's own pride; some read it as a name for God.
b: Ge'on means "pride" or "majesty". Hosea 5:5 and 7:10 say that Israel's pride "testifies to his face". The usual reading is that the nation's own arrogance bears witness against it. A few commentators take "the Pride of Israel" as a title of God, as Amos 8:7 may do with "the Pride of Jacob" (the LORD swears by it). The Greek has "the pride of Israel will be humbled", a different verb with the same consonants as "testify". The Plain English Translation keeps "testifies" and offers the Greek in the variant.

t: Seeking the LORD with sacrifices and not finding him
p: Sacrifice without a changed life does not reach him: he has "pulled away".
b: The flocks and herds are the sacrifices. The prophets say the same elsewhere: Isaiah 1:11-15 ("What use to me are all your many sacrifices?"), Micah 6:6-8 and Amos 5:21-24. Proverbs 1:28 has wisdom say of those who ignore her, "they will hunt hard for me and never find me." The verb chalats ("pulled away", "drawn off") is the word for taking a sandal off or pulling free; the LORD has taken himself out of their reach. Compare the nearby 5:15, where he stays away until they seek him from need.
r: Isaiah 1:11; Micah 6:6; Amos 5:21; Proverbs 1:28; Hosea 5:15; Hosea 6:6

p: The Hebrew zarim means foreign or outside; the children are born outside the LORD's family.
b: Zar is "stranger", "outsider" or "foreign", and a "foreign" thing is one outside the circle where it should be (Leviticus 10:1, "strange fire"). The "children" are the next generation, brought up in the cults of 4:13-14, or literally children of other fathers. Both fit the picture of the faithless wife in chapters 1 to 3. The line is a deeper form of "children of prostitution" (2:4). "New moon" in the next line is also the day of a feast, and the Greek reads "blight" (see the variant).

a: Blow the ram's horn in Gibeah
t: The alarm in Benjamin: the Syro-Ephraimite war?
p: Gibeah, Ramah and Beth-aven are towns on the road north of Jerusalem; the alarm may date to the war of 735-732 BC.
b: The alarm sounds in three towns of Benjamin, the border land between Judah and Israel: Gibeah (Tell el-Ful), Ramah (er-Ram) and Beth-aven (Bethel). Albrecht Alt (1919) argued that 5:8-6:6 reflects the Syro-Ephraimite war, when Aram and Israel attacked Ahaz of Judah (Isaiah 7:1-2; 2 Kings 16:5) and Judah took back Benjamin's border towns afterward; the verses on boundary stones (5:10) and on Ephraim's turning to Assyria (5:13) fit that time. Others see an earlier border clash. The Plain English Translation does not fix the occasion. Gibeah also recalls the crime of Judges 19 (Hosea 9:9; 10:9).
r: Isaiah 7:1; Isaiah 10:28; 2 Kings 16:5; Judges 19:22; Hosea 9:9; Hosea 10:9

p: The words match a war cry in Judges 5:14; the speaker may be Ephraim's army coming from behind.
b: 'Acharekha Binyamin is literally "behind you, Benjamin". Judges 5:14 says, "Benjamin came behind you, among your troops", in Deborah's song, where it describes Benjamin following Ephraim into battle. So the Hebrew may be the old war cry of the tribe, and Hosea repeats it: "Behind you, Benjamin!" may be Ephraim's army calling as it comes. Others read it as a warning that the enemy is behind Benjamin. The alarm is the same: war is on the border.

p: Moving a neighbor's marker is forbidden land-grabbing; Judah's leaders are accused of doing it.
b: "Do not move your neighbor's boundary marker" (Deuteronomy 19:14; compare Deuteronomy 27:17 and Proverbs 22:28) protected the family land that each household received. To move it was to steal land. Hosea's charge against Judah's princes is either a grab of territory from Ephraim in the aftermath of war (5:8) or a land-grab from the poor, as Isaiah 5:8 and Micah 2:2 describe. The LORD's answer is that he will pour out his wrath "like water", a flood no marker can stop.

p: Yareb may be a name, a title ("great king") or a nickname ("the king who fights").
b: No Assyrian king is named Jareb. Explanations: (1) a title, "great king", read rav (compare the Assyrian title "great king" and Isaiah 36:4); (2) "the king who contends", from riv, a nickname for Assyria's king; (3) a misspelling or a word used for a particular king, such as Tiglath-pileser III (745-727 BC). The same name is in 10:6. The Greek writes it as a name, "Iareim". The historical background is that Menahem paid tribute to Pul (2 Kings 15:19-20), Ahaz sent to Tiglath-pileser, "I am your servant and your son. Come up!" (2 Kings 16:7), and Hoshea paid tribute (2 Kings 17:3).

p: God compares himself to a lion, a young lion, a moth and rot: a destroyer of his own people.
b: In 5:12 the LORD is a moth and rot, small things that destroy slowly (compare Isaiah 50:9; Job 13:28); in 5:14 a lion and a young lion, which tear and carry off. Both verses say "like" in the Hebrew (a simile, not "I am a moth"). The Greek of 5:12 has "disturbance" (tarachē) and "goad" (kentron) for "moth" and "rot". The two Hebrew words of 5:14 are shachal and kefir. The picture comes back at 13:7-8, and Amos 1:2 and 3:8 have the LORD roaring as a lion. The warrior of the Exodus now fights Israel (Deuteronomy 32:39, "no one can pull anyone out of my hand"). The Plain English Translation does not soften it. Compare the repair of 6:1, "he tore us apart, and he will heal us".
r: Isaiah 50:9; Amos 1:2; Amos 3:8; Hosea 6:1; Hosea 13:7; Deuteronomy 32:39

a: until they pay for their guilt
t: "Pay for their guilt" and "seek me early"
p: 'Asham means to be guilty and to make amends; shachar is the dawn, so "seek me" means seek eagerly.
b: The verb 'asham means to be held guilty and, from there, to bear the consequence or make amends (compare the guilt offering, 'asham, Leviticus 5:14-19). The LORD withdraws "to my place" until they do. The last verb, yeshacharunni, comes from shachar, "dawn", and means to search for me early, eagerly. The play on the dawn comes back in 6:3 ("as sure as the dawn") and 6:4 (the morning cloud), where it describes what they promise and how short it lasts.

a: Come, let us turn back to the LORD
t: Who is speaking in 6:1-3, and do they mean it?
p: Some read the words as a genuine return, some as a shallow one that the LORD rejects in 6:4.
b: Three readings. (1) A sincere call by the prophet or the remnant (many Jewish and older Christian readers; the Targum and Jerome take it as the people repenting). (2) A hollow liturgy: the words are what the people say, but 6:4 and 7:14 show they are not meant (a common reading among modern commentators; Wolff treats it as a penitential liturgy used by the people). (3) A mixture: good words, the wrong reason, and a view of God as a healer on call. The Plain English Translation translates "turn back" (shuv) as in Jeremiah 3:12, 22, and the connection between this call and the LORD's "I will go away and go back to my place" (5:15) is part of the puzzle. The Greek introduces the song differently: "In their trouble they will seek me early, saying" (En thlipsei autōn orthriousi pros me legontes), so there the LORD quotes their words.

t: "After two days" and "on the third day"
p: The pattern "two days, on the third" is a Hebrew way to say a short time, with the third day as the turning point.
b: Hebrew often counts "two ... and the third" (compare "for three sins, even for four", Amos 1:3) to say that something happens soon, after a short interval. The third day is also the day when God acts in several stories (Genesis 22:4; 42:18; Exodus 19:11, 16; Esther 5:1). The Hebrew mi-yomayim is "from two days", that is, "after two days", as the Greek has it (meta dyo hēmeras). The revival comes after the second day, on the third, and the Plain English Translation says "after two days". The brevity is the point: the people expect the LORD's anger to be over almost at once, as 6:4 will show it is not. Genesis Rabbah 56:1 collects "third day" verses and counts this one among them.

p: The usual reading is national recovery; the Targum and many Christians heard resurrection.
b: The usual critical reading: the verbs go with the image of illness and healing (6:1). The people hope that God will give them life again as a sick person lives again, a national recovery; Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37) uses the same picture for the nation. The Targum says "on the day of the resurrection of the dead he will raise us up". Christian readers (Jerome; Cyril of Alexandria) took it as Christ's resurrection on the third day, since Paul says he rose "according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:4) and Luke 24:46 says it stands written, though neither names Hosea. Some critical scholars have proposed that the song borrows the pattern of a dying and rising fertility god, an idea Hosea would then be rejecting; this site has not checked who holds this view, so no one is named. The Greek has "he will heal us" (hygiasei hēmas) and "we will rise" (anastēsometha), the verb the New Testament uses for rising from the dead. See the card below.
r: Ezekiel 37:12; Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; Luke 24:46; 1 Corinthians 15:4; Hosea 13:14

a: let us chase after knowing the LORD
p: To know the LORD is the goal of 6:3, and the picture is a sure dawn and a soaking spring rain.
b: The verb "chase" (radaf) is the verb of pursuit in war (Joshua 2:5). It joins with "know" in a strong phrase: to run after knowing God. The two similes are the dawn that never fails and the rain: the heavy winter rain and the "spring rain" (malqosh), the late rain that fills the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14; Joel 2:23). Hosea ends the book with God as the dew (14:5). In Canaanite belief the rain was Baal's gift (see the note at 2:5), so the people are asking the LORD to give them what they had looked for elsewhere.
r: Deuteronomy 11:14; Joel 2:23; Jeremiah 5:24; Hosea 2:21; Hosea 10:12; Hosea 14:5

a: Your loyal love is like a morning cloud
p: The same word hesed that is the LORD's greatest quality is here the people's, and it disappears with the dew.
b: The LORD answers the call of 6:1-3 with two questions. The people's hesed, "loyal love", is like a morning cloud and early dew, gone when the sun rises. In 6:6 the LORD says that hesed is what he wants. So the same word marks what the LORD gives, what the people owe him and what they fail to give (4:1). The line "What can I do with you?" is a sign of anguish, not anger; compare 11:8, "How can I give you up, Ephraim?".

a: hacked at them through the prophets
p: The prophets' words cut like an axe; Jeremiah's call (Jeremiah 1:10) says the same.
b: Chatsav means to hew stone or cut wood (Isaiah 51:1). Here God's word, spoken by prophets, hacks and kills. Jeremiah's call (Jeremiah 1:10) makes him a prophet "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish", and Jeremiah 5:14 has God make his words a fire. Hosea himself says that the prophet is "a fool" in the eyes of the people (9:7). The judgment of the LORD "goes out like light" in the Greek, which the Plain English Translation follows; see the variant.

a: Loyal love is what I want
p: Hosea 6:6 is quoted by Jesus twice; its "not ... but" means "more than", not "instead of".
b: Hesed is covenant faithfulness to God and neighbor. The Greek renders it eleos, "mercy", and Matthew gives Jesus the same noun, eleos, with his own "and not" where Swete's Greek has "rather than": "Mercy is what I want, not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7). The Hebrew "not X but Y" is often a comparison, as the parallel line shows ("more than burnt offerings"), and the same idea is in 1 Samuel 15:22 ("listening is better than sacrifice"), Micah 6:6-8 and Psalm 40:6. Most scholars think the prophets did not abolish sacrifice but ranked it below faithful living. Others (older critics such as Wellhausen) saw the prophets as opposed to the cult itself. The Plain English Translation's "Loyal love" matches 4:1 and 6:4.
orig: כִּי חֶסֶד חָפַצְתִּי וְלֹא־זָבַח (ki chesed chafatsti velo'-zavach)
r: Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7; 1 Samuel 15:22; Micah 6:6; Isaiah 1:11; Psalm 40:6

a: But they, like Adam, overstepped the covenant
t: "Like Adam": a man, the first man, or a town?
p: The Hebrew ke'adam can be "like Adam", "like humankind" or "at Adam" (a town in the Jordan valley).
b: Three readings. (1) The first man: Adam broke a covenant-like command in Eden. Some Jewish and Christian readers take it this way (this site has not checked which commentators), and covenant theology has used the verse to argue that Adam was in a covenant with God. (2) "Like human beings": they act like ordinary people, not like a people of the covenant (the Greek has "like a man"). (3) "At Adam": a town on the Jordan (Joshua 3:16), with "there" in the next line pointing to a place. Gilead and Shechem follow in 6:8-9, so a list of places is plausible. The Hebrew allows all three, and the Plain English Translation keeps "like Adam".

t: Gilead, a town stained with blood
p: Gilead lay east of the Jordan; Pekah's revolt began there with fifty Gileadites.
b: Gilead is the high country east of the Jordan, and here a town of that name, perhaps Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22) or Mizpah-gilead. Its mention with Shechem in the next verse and Pekah's coup with fifty Gileadites (2 Kings 15:25) lead some to link the "tracks of blood" with that murder or with Jeroboam II's wars. The Hebrew 'aqovah may mean "tracked" or "crooked" (from 'aqov, tricky). The Greek reads "stirring up water". The Plain English Translation says "marked with the tracks of blood", which is the common meaning, and no event is named.

a: murders along the road to Shechem
t: Priests who murder on the road to Shechem
p: A band of priests kills travelers on a road to Shechem; the event is unknown.
b: Shechem was a city of refuge and a Levitical town in Ephraim (Joshua 20:7; 21:21) where the covenant was renewed (Joshua 24). A gang of priests murdering on the road to it recalls an ambush; if the road led to a sanctuary, they may have preyed on pilgrims. The Hebrew of the first half is unclear: chakkei ish gedudim chever kohanim, "the waiting of a man, bands; a company of priests". The Greek says "priests hid the way and killed Shechem". The Plain English Translation gives the simplest sense and notes that nothing in the text names the crime outside this verse.

a: when I turn my people's fortunes around
p: A harvest is set for Judah: of judgment or blessing, depending on the reading.
b: Shuv shevut is the phrase Jeremiah uses of the return from exile (Jeremiah 29:14): "I will turn your fortunes around". It may come from shevut, "captivity", which the Greek reads ("I turn back the captivity"). The "harvest" is either judgment, as in Joel 3:13 and Jeremiah 51:33, or the fruit of restoration. The line stands at the end of the section on Judah (5:8-6:11) and before 7:1, "Each time I try to heal Israel". Reading it with 7:1, as the Greek does, links the restoration of fortunes to the healing.

p: Samaria, Omri's city on its hill, was the capital of the north; it stands for the whole kingdom's rulers.
b: Omri bought the hill and built Samaria as the capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:24). Hosea names it with Ephraim here and in 8:5-6, 10:5-7 and 13:16, where its fall is told plainly. In his time the city was the seat of a succession of kings, most of whom reigned only a short time; Assyria besieged it for three years and took it in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5-6). "Samaria" can mean the city, its government or the nation. See the topic on Samaria.

a: like an oven the baker keeps burning
p: Chapter 7 compares the plotters to an oven; the oven image is hard to follow, and the text may be damaged.
b: A village oven was a clay pot or pit heated with wood. The adulterers (the word of 4:2 and 4:13-14) burn like an oven that the baker keeps hot, stopping only while the dough rises; a night of scheming lets the fire go out until morning (7:6). The Hebrew has several unclear words, and commentators move or change some. The picture is of slow-heating passion that waits for its moment, a coup. The Plain English Translation does not change the text.

t: The king's day, wine and mockers
p: A royal feast day, drinking, and mockers: the scene may be a coup under cover of a banquet.
b: "The day of our king" may be his enthronement day or birthday (Genesis 40:20 mentions Pharaoh's birthday). The princes make themselves ill with the "heat" of wine, and the king, drunk himself, "stretches out his hand with scoffers" (shakes hands or joins them). The scene is the setting for a plot, as in 7:3-7, where kings fall. Wine and drinking appear in the same verses as treachery in 7:5 and 4:11. The Hebrew subject of "stretches out" is not named, so the king is assumed.

p: The Hebrew 'ophehem ("their baker") may have been 'appam ("their anger"), which the Greek seems to suggest.
b: The Hebrew is 'ophehem, "their baker", and the whole passage keeps the baker image. A different vowel and consonant give 'appam, "their anger", and "all night their anger sleeps; in the morning it burns like a flaming fire" reads more smoothly. Some scholars adopt it; the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and the baker (the Greek in Swete's edition reads "all night Ephraim was filled with sleep", hypnou Ephraim eneplēsthē). Either way the plotting heart is a banked oven that bursts into flame at dawn.

p: Four of Israel's last six kings were murdered by their successors.
b: After Jeroboam II, Israel's kings came and went by murder. Shallum killed Zechariah (2 Kings 15:10): "He struck him down in front of the people and killed him." Menahem killed Shallum (15:14); Pekah killed Pekahiah (15:25); and Hoshea "formed a plot against Pekah son of Remaliah" (15:30). So "they devour their rulers" is close to a list of events, and "not one calls to me" says that no king, coup or party turned to the LORD. Most scholars place this chapter between 745 and 732 BC.
r: 2 Kings 15:10; 2 Kings 15:14; 2 Kings 15:25; 2 Kings 15:30; Hosea 8:4; Hosea 13:10

p: Ephraim blends with the peoples like flour with oil; Psalm 106:35 says the same of earlier Israel.
b: Yitbolal is "he mixes himself", the verb used for flour mixed with oil in an offering (Leviticus 2:5). Psalm 106:35 says of Israel, "They mixed in among the nations and picked up their practices." The "flat loaf, not turned over" ('ugah, a cake baked on hot stones) is burnt on one side and raw on the other: a nation half-baked and spoiled. The point is that Ephraim has neither a clear identity nor the strength to keep one.

t: Gray hairs he has not noticed
p: Ephraim is aging and weak and does not know it; foreign powers have drained him.
b: "Foreigners have consumed his strength" is a picture of tribute and loss (Menahem's silver to Assyria, 2 Kings 15:19-20, and the treaty-payments that followed) and the "gray hairs" are the first signs of death, which a man in denial does not see. The refrain "he has not noticed" (literally "does not know") links to 5:4 and 4:1: the nation does not know the LORD and does not know its own state.

p: Israel's last kings asked help from both Egypt and Assyria; Hoshea tried both.
b: A dove is a bird that flies back and forth with no plan. Menahem and Hoshea both turned to Assyria; Hoshea also sent to So, king of Egypt, and stopped paying tribute, and Assyria shut him up (2 Kings 17:3-4). Hosea returns to this double game in 5:13, 8:9 and 12:1. The word for "silly", pothah, is the word for a gullible, naive person (Proverbs 7:7, "the naive"). The alliance is described in the book's own words as "lovers" (2:5; 8:9).
r: 2 Kings 17:3; 2 Kings 17:4; Proverbs 7:7; Hosea 5:13; Hosea 8:9; Hosea 12:1

t: "As the warning to their assembly said"
p: The Hebrew is uncertain: a report, a hearing or an announcement made to the assembly.
b: Kesheima' la'adatam is "according to the report to their assembly" or "as the hearing for their assembly". Most commentators think it means the covenant curses that were read aloud to the assembly (Deuteronomy 28; 31:11-13): the LORD will do as he warned. The Greek has "in the hearing of their distress". The "net" and the "birds" (7:12) also bring back the trap of 5:1: the hunter has become the LORD.

t: "I would redeem them": a wish, or a fact?
p: The verb pada (redeem) can mean "I redeemed them" (the exodus) or "I would redeem them".
b: Pada is the word of the exodus, the LORD "redeeming" Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8; 15:15). The Hebrew form here can mean "I redeemed them" or "I would redeem them", a wish held back. The Greek says "I redeemed them". The Plain English Translation's "would" shows that the LORD is on the edge of acting. At 13:14 the same verb appears in a hard question, "Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol?". Compare also 11:8. The "woe" word in this verse is 'oy, a cry of pain, not the prophets' hoy.

p: A bow that does not shoot straight is a picture of a people that will fail when it is needed.
b: The "slack" or "deceitful" bow (qeshet remiyyah) is a bow that shoots wide or breaks. Psalm 78:57 says Israel "warped like a bow that cannot be trusted". The lines on turning, "They turn, but not upward", are uncertain (see the variant). The last line, "in the land of Egypt", looks back to the call to Egypt in 7:11 and ahead to the threat of return to Egypt in 8:13 and 9:3, 6. The princes' "rage of their tongues" may be cursing or boasting.
